title: FinHarness: An Inline Lifecycle Safety Harness for Finance LLM Agents
abstract: Finance LLM agents must simultaneously block prompt-induced unauthorized actions and approve legitimate multi-step business workflows. However, boundary filters often miss irreversible mid-trajectory tool calls, while post-hoc LLM judges perform auditing only after termination -- too late for intervention and at a computational cost that scales linearly with trace length. We present FinHarness, an inline safety harness that wraps a finance agent end-to-end with three components: a Query Monitor that fuses single-turn intent with cross-turn drift, a Tool Monitor that evaluates each prospective tool call, and a Cascade module that integrates per-step risk and adaptively routes verification between a lightweight and an advanced-tier LLM judge. Fired risk factors are re-injected into the agent input as ex-ante evidence, enabling the agent to refuse, re-plan, or approve on its own. On FinVault, routed FinHarness cuts ASR from 38.3% to 15.0% while largely preserving benign approval ($41.1\% \to 39.3\%$), and uses $4.7\times$ fewer advanced-judge calls than an always-advanced ablation.

significance.justification: The paper addresses a critical safety challenge for finance LLM agents by introducing an inline safety harness that reduces attack success rate from 38.3% to 15.0% while preserving legitimate workflow approvals, directly impacting how builders implement safety mechanisms for production LLM systems.

novelty.justification: FinHarness introduces a novel inline approach that fuses single-turn intent with cross-turn drift detection and adaptive routing between lightweight and advanced LLM judges, representing a substantial variation from traditional boundary filters or post-hoc auditing methods.

reproducibility.justification: The method is described clearly with three distinct components and evaluation on FinVault benchmark, but the paper does not mention code or dataset availability, requiring reimplementation from the description.

clarity.justification: The paper is well-structured with clear problem framing, method description, and quantitative results showing significant safety improvements with computational efficiency gains (4.7× fewer advanced-judge calls).

topical_fit.justification: The paper directly addresses LLM safety and deployment challenges for financial applications, making it highly relevant for builders implementing production LLM systems with safety requirements.
